seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July, while seasonal snow still covers the Colchuck Glacier to the col and before it melts to hard bare ice

July.reason: Continuous consolidated snow up the glacier to the col takes crampons well, and the Class 2-3 ridge above is mostly melted out.

June.reason: The access road may still be closed and the glacier gully holds deep, avalanche-prone snow; the scramble ridge above the col can still be snow-covered.

August.reason: Snow on the glacier thins and gets suncupped; patches of hard ice near the col become more likely late in the month, so crampons are essential.

October.reason: Fresh snow over bare glacier ice, short days and freezing temperatures make the glacier and col treacherous; the access road can close with the first heavy snow.

September.reason: Seasonal snow is often gone, leaving bare glacier ice at the 40-degree section below the col where crampons bite poorly and a slip is hard to stop.

best_season: Late July through September; snow persists longer on north slopes

season: Year-round; best Jun-Sep (ice axe can help in shoulder-season snow)

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: March to April, when the north face ice is fat and the Coleman Glacier crevasses are still well bridged

May.reason: Warming loosens the rock steps and ice, raising rockfall, and bridges on the Coleman Glacier soften; go only after a cold spell and start very early.

June.reason: The ice on the rock steps rots and sheds, rockfall increases, and large crevasses can open across the Coleman Glacier.

April.reason: Longer days and a shrinking snowline on the road, with the face's ice and mixed steps still frozen in; skis help on the approach and descent.

March.reason: The north face ice is usually well formed and crevasse bridges are solid, but the approach often still starts miles down the snowbound road.

February.reason: The unplowed Glacier Creek Road adds miles of snow travel, short days squeeze a long approach, and storm slabs load the slopes above the Coleman Glacier.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July to early September, once the talus gully to the notch has melted out and the serpentine is dry

May.reason: Late May ascents happen, but the approach gully is full snow, hard in the morning and prone to wet slides as it warms.

July.reason: Snow in the gully shrinks to short patches and the slick serpentine dries; the Ingalls Way trailhead lot fills early on weekends.

June.reason: The gully still holds snow needing axe and crampons early, then good plunge-stepping; the upper ridge rock is usually dry by late June.

August.reason: Snow-free loose talus to the notch and dry rock; more parties above in the gully raises rockfall risk, so start early.

October.reason: Early snow and verglas on the serpentine make the squeeze and downclimbs treacherous, and the rappel descent slows in cold.

September.reason: Larches turn and crowds peak on the Ingalls Way trail; dry rock but shorter days on a long 14-16 hour outing.

season: Year-round (winter ascents documented); best scrambling conditions Jul-Sep

best_season: Climbed in July and August; the basin's approach terrain holds snow into early summer at this elevation and the brush is markedly worse when wet, so a stretch of settled, dry weather is recommended.

season: Jun-Sep (snow lingers on approach benches into early July; class 2-3 talus mostly melts out by late Jul-Aug)

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Early July to early August, while snow bridges over crevasses and the moats below the summit blocks are still solid

July.reason: Consolidated snow bridges and filled moats make the glacier travel and summit blocks straightforward, with long days for the traverse.

June.reason: Deep snow cover bridges the crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers; the Eldorado Creek basin slopes can still slide after warm spells.

August.reason: Crevasses on the McAllister and Klawatti glaciers open and moats widen through the month; water on the glaciers becomes scarce.

October.reason: Fresh snow over open crevasses hides them, days are short, and the Cascade River Road is gated at the Eldorado trailhead in late autumn.

September.reason: Open crevasses, bare ice and widened bergschrunds complicate the traverse and summit access, and early autumn storms can bring whiteout.

best_season: July to early August, while snow bridges over crevasses and moats are still solid

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, when the south gully and talus are snow-free and the Nason Ridge trail is dry for a long day

May.reason: A spring snow climb: consolidated snow fills the gullies and the Rock-Crescent col, but cornices and wet slough threaten the col; axe and crampons.

July.reason: The talus and the class 3 gully melt out through the month; early July can still need an axe on the col and in the gully.

June.reason: Snow lingers above about 5,000 ft on the Rock Lake side and softens into slush by midday; the col can still carry a cornice.

August.reason: The route is snow-free talus and trail, Crescent Lake is the only reliable water, and blueberries line the overgrown Nason Ridge trail.

October.reason: The first snow can coat the loose south gully and the talus, and short days make the round trip tight.

September.reason: Cooler days suit the 3,300 ft climb to Crescent Lake, the rock is dry, and fall color comes to Nason Ridge.

season: Aug-Oct (best after snowmelt; blueberry and fall-color season in the Bathtub Lakes basin is a noted highlight; spring travel requires ice axe/crampons)
Jul-Oct (trail typically snow-covered into early/midsummer some years)
Jul-Aug (dry rock across all three summits; earlier season has more snow/rockfall risk, later season has minimal water)
Jun-Oct (summer scramble); also documented as a January ski-mountaineering ascent
Jun-Oct (one of the first higher hikes in the area to lose its winter snowpack; ridge crest and Nine-mile Saddle can still hold snow in early season)
Late May-early June (best on consolidated, not-yet-melted-out snow)
Jul-Sep (dry rock); scrambling feasible into Jun/Oct with snow on the approach
Jun-Sep (early-season ascents require ice axe/crampons for snow in the gully)
